Quality Power: Quietly Building a Global Energy-Transition Stack

Quality Power Electrical Equipments is emerging as a differentiated way to play the global energy-transition and grid-modernisation cycle.

2. Business - What they sell

High-voltage and power-quality equipment that is essential for:
a) Moving power long distances (HVAC/HVDC)
b) Keeping grids stable
c) Protecting expensive equipment
d)  Making industrial power cheaper and more reliable

Why customers care
A failure in these products doesn’t just mean replacing a part – it can mean grid problems, plant shutdowns and big financial losses. That’s why approvals, test labs and track record matter so much, and why this part of the value chain can be quite attractive for investors.

Who they sell to
Global equipment makers (GE, Siemens, Hitachi, etc.), utilities (PGCIL, state discoms), and large industrial customers

3. Moat: Why This Franchise Is Hard to Replicate
3.1 Approvals and track record with blue chip customers
a) Quality Power is already approved with top global OEMs and utilities (GE, Siemens, Hitachi, Hyosung, PGCIL, etc.).

b) Getting onto these vendor lists for HVDC/FACTS and high voltage equipment takes years of design validation, type tests and field performance.

c) Once approved, customers are reluctant to switch because failure risk is high – this creates sticky, repeat business.

3.2 NABL accredited high voltage test labs (up to 765 KV)
a) This allows in house type testing to Indian and international standards, speeds up product development and reduces dependence on external labs.

b) For a new entrant, building similar test infrastructure and getting accreditation is capital intensive and time consuming.

3.3 Technically demanding, niche product lines
a) Coils/reactors for HVDC and FACTS, and high voltage instrument transformers up to 500 kV, are not commodity products.

b) These are engineered, safety critical components where buyers prioritize reliability and proven performance over the last bit of price.

c) That keeps the competitive set limited and supports better pricing and margins than generic transformers.

3.4 Integrated product and solution stack
Through acquisitions (Endoks, Mehru, Sukrut, Nebeskie, etc.), Quality Power can now offer:
a) Coils/reactors + instrument transformers + accessories + composites

b) Plus power quality systems (SVC/STATCOM) and monitoring/analytics.

c) This lets the company capture a higher share of project value and makes it harder for a single product competitor to displace them.

3.5 Export footprint and diversification
a) A large share of revenue comes from exports across 100+ countries.

b) This diversifies demand beyond one geography and builds a reference base across multiple grid operators and industrial customers.

c) Over time, this global installed base itself becomes a moat – more references lead to more approvals and more orders.

In short, the moat here is a combination of long cycle approvals, specialised test and engineering capabilities, niche high voltage products and an integrated offering – not something a new player can easily recreate

4. Industry Tailwinds
4.1 Global grid capex is structurally rising
a) Power systems worldwide are being rebuilt for renewables, reliability and cross border trade.

b) The global electricity transmission market is expected to grow steadily over the next few years, adding tens of billions of dollars of spend on lines, substations, HV equipment and control systems.

c) This is long cycle, policy backed capex – not a short term theme.

4.2 HVDC and FACTS moving from niche to mainstream
1) As grids integrate more solar and wind, they need:
a) HVDC lines to move power efficiently over long distances.
b) FACTS systems (SVCs, STATCOMs, advanced filters) to keep voltage stable and improve power quality.

2) Market estimates point to high teens growth in HVDC/FACTS spend over the medium term, especially in markets like India, the Middle East, US and Europe.[

These are exactly the projects that require coils/reactors, instrument transformers and power quality systems that Quality Power supplies.

4.3 India’s grid upgrade is a multi year story by itself
a) India’s transmission network and substation capacity have been expanding steadily, with dozens of projects under construction at any point in time

b) The government has laid out an ambitious roadmap for renewable additions and inter regional transmission corridors, including a sizeable HVDC pipeline.

This creates a domestic demand layer on top of export opportunities.

4.4 Industrial power quality demand is rising

Large industrial users (steel, cement, refineries, data centres, rail, autos) are facing:
a) Stricter grid code and power quality norms.
b) Higher penalties for poor power factor and harmonics.

This pushes them to invest in reactors, filters, capacitor banks and STATCOM/SVC solutions – all areas where Quality Power is present.

Overall Takeaway: For a company like Quality Power, sitting on the component and systems side of transmission, HVDC/FACTS and power quality, these tailwinds translate into a long, visible opportunity set – provided it can execute and scale responsibly.

5. Financial Performance: High Growth, High Margins
Recent reported numbers highlight a sharp inflection:

Q3 FY26 (YoY)
Revenue: 28.43 cr (+256.5%)
EBITDA: 7.93 cr (+222.7%)
PAT: ₹6.28 cr (+220.7%)
Margins: Gross 42.3%, EBITDA 27.9%, PAT 22.1%

9M FY26 (YoY)
Revenue: 69.72 cr (+165.7%)
EBITDA: 17.70 cr (+112.8%)
PAT: 13.50 cr (+93.8%)
 Margins: Gross 41.9%, EBITDA 25.4%, PAT 19.4%

On a multi-year view, revenue has compounded strongly, while EBITDA and PAT margins have expanded as mix improves (more HVDC/FACTS, Mehru ramp), scale benefits kick in and acquisitions contribute.

ROCE: 37.3% (FY23) → 36.1% (FY24) → 29.2% (FY25) → 23.1% (H1 FY26)

ROE: 23.6% → 30.2% → 25.5% → 19.7% over the same periods

There is some moderation as capital employed bulks up with Mehru site and new capex, but returns remain comfortably above cost of capital.

Cash flow caveat
One key caveat: cash conversion has weakened. CFO/EBITDA ratios have trended down as working capital absorbed cash during the growth and capex ramp, with H1 FY26 CFO turning negative. This is not unusual in a project-heavy export business, but it is an important monitorable.

6. Capex Cycle: Building for the Next Leg of Growth
Global Coil Factory – Sangli (Kupwad MIDC) - 
a) One of the largest coil/reactor facilities globally, designed for up to 8x current coil capacity, along with a 2,500 kV AC high-power test lab.

b)  Timelines have been advanced; key construction milestones are now targeted around mid-2026, with full project completion by Q2 FY27.

Cochin (Aluva) expansion
a) Capacity effectively doubled for dry-type coils and related equipment.
b) Includes a new MV test lab; this expansion has already been completed.

Mehru – Bhiwadi expansion
a) new autoclaves and layout changes expected to increase capacity by ~45%.
b) Phased commissioning, with completion around FY26.

HVDC CTC magnet-wire facility
Backward integration into specialised CTC conductors for HVDC windings, now under implementation.

Global Engineering & Technology Centre
Board-approved ~₹25 crore capex for a centralised engineering and design hub at Sangli.[1]

On the funding side, the 2025 IPO brought in fresh equity to fund the Mehru acquisition and part of the capex, while adding a buffer for future M&A and general corporate purposes. Current leverage is low (debt-to-equity about 0.05x as of H1 FY26), leaving ample headroom to support growth if required.

Overall, the announced capex appears well within the company’s funding capacity when combining IPO proceeds, internal accruals and moderate potential leverage

7. Strategy and Growth Drivers

Management’s articulated priorities can be summarised as:

7.1 Technology-led, export-oriented growth: Focus on HVDC, FACTS, STATCOM and high-voltage AC components, with Turkey and global coil factory as export hubs.

7.2 Deeper value-chain participation: Moving from coils alone to instrument transformers, accessories, composites, and digital/analytics – increasing project wallet share.

7.3 Capacity ahead of demand: Building capacity proactively in coils, transformers and instrument transformers to capture a larger share of the upcoming grid capex cycle.

7.4 Disciplined execution: Emphasis on material planning, project oversight and cost control to maintain healthy profitability in a lumpy project environment.

The order book of over 895. cr provides near-term visibility and supports the case for continued scale-up if execution remains disciplined.

8. Key Risks

Investors and observers should keep an eye on:

8.1 Working capital and cash flows: Sustained revenue growth with weak cash conversion can force higher reliance on debt or equity.

8.2 Execution risk on multiple capex projects: Sangli coil factory, Mehru expansion and HVDC magnet-wire line all need to be commissioned and ramped without major delays or cost overruns.

8.3 Integration risk: Mehru, Endoks, Sukrut and other acquisitions must deliver on synergy and margin expectations.

8.4 Project and customer concentration: A few large OEMs and utilities contribute a significant share of order book; any loss of share or project delays can impact growth and margins.

8.5 Margin normalisation: Current margin profile is strong; competitive intensity, commodity price swings or mix changes could drive volatility.

9. Valuation Lens

It is fair to say that the market is already pricing in a significant amount of optimism. The stock trades at valuations that are quite elevated relative to traditional capital-goods names and to its own short listed history.

For new capital, this implies that the margin of safety is not very high at present levels. The thesis becomes more execution-sensitive: any disappointment on order inflows, cash flows or capex timelines can lead to sharp de-rating, while clean execution through FY27 could sustain or even justify rich valuations.

10. Closing Thoughts

Quality Power represents a differentiated way to participate in the global energy-transition and grid-modernisation theme: a technically strong, export-oriented, high-voltage equipment franchise with a growing product stack and high return ratios. 

The capex being executed today is clearly aimed at making the company a much larger player in coils/reactors, instrument transformers and power-quality systems over the next cycle.

At the same time, the bar set by current valuations is high. For anyone tracking the name, the focus over the next 6–12 quarters should be on three things:

a) order inflows (especially in HVDC/FACTS)
b)  cash-flow quality (CFO vs EBITDA)
c) progress on large capex projects

How the company navigates these will decide whether the current valuation premium proves justified or stretched.
